causalModel.founding: Rebuilt after the Slaughter of 4E 48 on the best natural harbour of the south coast, smaller and lower than the city it replaced.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: A firm crest above a shallow shelf: the stilt quarters step down from the crest to a tidal flat and a lighter quay. Big hulls anchor out on the 10 m plateau and their cargo comes ashore by lighter. The lightering is the city’s living.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: A reconstituted merchant council governs by tariff; it will not appoint a ruler. The last party that had one killed the city.
causalModel.pressures: Hostile to the An-Xileel successor state and indispensable to a bay that must trade somewhere. It is also built over its own mass grave.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: If the third Hist ever spoke to one faction alone, every institution here would break at once. The rules forbid it.

scaleGrounding.loreSource: settlement-register.md §2 (M5, rebuilt smaller); lilmoth.md owner decision 2026-08-24 (smaller, lower, over a mass grave); 95-build-sequence.md (M5 quest band 35–60); Morrowind:Balmora as the ratio check at about 40 buildings.
scaleGrounding.why: Twenty-six households in bamboo huts and the tall block, at five to a household, give about 130 residents; the council, the patrol, the tenders, the licence and salvage staff and the lighter crews housed on the quay add 60 to 100 more. Fifty-three placed structures is a third more than Balmora’s forty, which is the right size for a major city rebuilt smaller than the one that it replaced. Seventy named residents follows Morrowind’s ratio of named people to buildings.

candidates.why: The east face of the promontory. Section from the crest out: 21.9 m at 3640/6350, a 22.5° bluff, a 7.4 m bench at 3720/6350 (slope 2.5°), a tidal flat at 1.3–1.5 m from 3800 to 3860 (flood band 1–3, wet-season inundated), then 1.0 m of water at 3880, 3.8 m at 3920 and a 6.6 m roadstead plateau from 3960 to 4040. That is four buildable tiers and a drowned quarter in one 400 m run. The shallow shelf is 120 m wide, which is why large hulls anchor out and their cargo comes ashore by lighter (Lore:Lilmoth). 55 m from the approved anchor, well inside its 0.04 UV (296 m) tolerance.

candidates.rejectedBecause: The south-east embayment reaches 3.8 m of water 50 m off the shore and 15.5 m at 150 m. Deep water that close means a hull could berth alongside, which contradicts the record in Lore:Lilmoth that the city is built over shallow water and lighters its cargo. It also has no bench between the shore and the crest, so the city would be one tier, not three.
candidates.why: Shore at roughly 3790/6540, water 0.6 m at 3798/6548, 3.8 m at 3826/6576, 9.6 m at 3855/6605, 25.5 m at 3939/6689; the SE ray falls 18.6 m to the waterline over 280 m with no flat step.

candidates.rejectedBecause: The southern lagoon behind the spit is 0.4–0.6 m deep at 3600/6590–6630 and land again at 3600/6670. Nothing there can be drowned to dive depth, so the drowned quarter, the record's signature, would be a puddle. No lighter could reach open water.
candidates.why: Sheltered water and a natural breakwater, which is why it was measured at all: 2.0 m of land at 3600/6510, 1.05 m at 3600/6550, 0.4 m of water at 3600/6590, land at 1.6 m again at 3600/6670.

districts.notes: What the water left standing: the arch across the road, the tower, two wall stubs and the rubble of the south tower. No new work is built into the masonry. Named for the road it faces (owner 2026-09-07); the district and socket ids keep the old survey name because ids are stable.

why.what: The Blackrose gate, which the city's old survey called the north gate: the Imperial arch, its surviving tower and the broken curtain either side, on the road from Blackrose.
why.whyHere: The Imperial circuit met its road here and the rebuilders kept the gate because it stood.
why.whyNeighbours: The Argonian track begins where the road ends inside it; the Hist court is on the crest above.
why.playerPurpose: The land entrance to the city, the patrol post and the north-gate station.
why.microGeography: A 14–16 m shelf between the pond on the west and the crest on the east, the lowest dry crossing of the wall line.

districts.notes: The crest, 19–23 m: the third Hist inside a ring of poles open to the east, two lodges outside the ring, the vigil awning inside it.

why.what: The Hist court: the tree, its ring of poles, the two tenders’ lodges and the vigil awning.
why.whyHere: The third tree grew from the second’s root on the crest. The city bends round it.
why.whyNeighbours: The spine track passes its east opening; the gate is below it to the west and the council bench to the east.
why.playerPurpose: The Hist court scene, the minder and the second tender.
why.microGeography: The highest ground in the city, level for 20 m round the trunk and falling on every side.

districts.notes: The 11–13 m bench east of the crest: hall, record room, strongroom, market deck, elders’ house, council floor, factor’s house and the bell on the lip. The hall and the market deck stand square to the bench walk; every other piece is set a few degrees off it on its own piles, following the fall of the bench, because an Argonian quarter is not surveyed (97 C8, Part F).

why.what: The council crown: the hall, the record room and strongroom, the open council floor, the upper market deck and the tariff bell.
why.whyHere: The merchant council needs level ground above the flood with the quay in view; the bench is the widest such ground.
why.whyNeighbours: The spine track arrives from the court on its west; the bluff stair leaves from the bell on its east.
why.playerPurpose: The council quests, the tariff roll, the upper market and the bell that is seen from the bay.
why.microGeography: A level 12 m shelf 80 m long, falling 1 m to the north and 2 m to the south.

districts.notes: The tidal flat under the bluff, 1–3 m, wet-season flooded. A loop of walkway with a cross lane, fifteen huts and the tall block, every one on piles.

why.what: Pusbottom: the repopulated slum on the flat under the bluff, a loop of planks with huts on both sides.
why.whyHere: The cheapest ground in the city is the ground that floods; the poor and the criminal quarter took it back after 4E 48.
why.whyNeighbours: The bell and the council stand on the bluff above it; the quay is along its east side.
why.playerPurpose: The vault, the slaughter list, the agent, the broker and most of the city’s dwellings.
why.microGeography: A flat at 1–3 m between the bluff foot and the water, drained by the lanes’ pile lines.

districts.notes: The water’s edge: the deck, the lamp, the licence house, the lighter shed, the divers’ shed and the salvage bench, with the pier and the stair.

why.what: The lighter quay: the deck at the water’s edge with the sheds along the lane behind it and the pier into the channel.
why.whyHere: Cargo comes ashore by lighter and the lighters need a deck, a light, a licence and a shed.
why.whyNeighbours: Pusbottom is at its back; the drowned quarter lies off its face.
why.playerPurpose: The lighter-quay station, the licences, the divers and the boat services.
why.microGeography: A strip of flat at 0–2 m along the shore, its east piles in the shallows.

districts.notes: The low flat south of the bluff: seven fishers’ huts in two rows on the shore lane, a boat awning, a drying rack and the pole wall facing the estuary.

why.what: The shore quarter: the fishers’ row on the low flat south of Pusbottom, behind the Argonian pole wall.
why.whyHere: The fishers of the estuary live on the flat nearest their water and away from the cargo quay.
why.whyNeighbours: Pusbottom is north-east across the shore lane; the pole wall closes it on the east.
why.playerPurpose: The offering season, the recitation speakers and a canoe for the estuary.
why.microGeography: A 2 m flat that floods in the wet season, drained toward the estuary.

districts.notes: Old Imperial Lilmoth under 1–12 m of water: seven ruin pieces on the old street grid, the shrine outermost, the channel cut through the middle.

why.what: The drowned quarter: the sunken Imperial villas off the quay, from the ridge in the shallows to the shrine on the plateau edge.
why.whyHere: Imperial houses on this soil sank; the rebuilders left the quarter drowned. No one has built on the ground since.
why.whyNeighbours: The quay and the diving stair are inshore; the roadstead is at its outer edge.
why.playerPurpose: The dive scene, the salvage quests and the shrine.
why.microGeography: The shelf falls from 1 m off the quay to 12 m at the plateau, with the channel dredged through it.

districts.notes: A one-piece works district: the roofed dues board beside the quay lane. The board is a works-v1 prop and the kit-set rule (one set per district) gives it a district of its own, three metres by seven, inside the quay's ground.

why.what: The dues board: the roofed notice board on which the licence house posts the lightering dues and the lot prices.
why.whyHere: Lilmoth lives by lightering. The dues are read by every crew before they go to the licence house window; the record's price list belongs in the open, not behind a door.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands across the quay lane from the licence house door and south of the quay lamp, on the line that every lighter crew walks from the deck to the stair.
why.playerPurpose: The prices and dues of Cargo Off the Ledger are read here. The board is where a forged notice can be pinned.
why.microGeography: Two driven posts on the dry flat at 2.3 m, a stride east of the lane planks and clear of the flood band.

parcels.orientationWhy: The arch is set square to the Blackwood-side road so the carriageway passes through its opening.

why.what: The surviving Imperial gate arch, 7.3 m of ashlar standing across the road from Blackrose.
why.whyHere: The Imperial circuit needed a landward gate where its road met the rise. The rebuilders kept the arch because it was still standing.
why.whySpot: The arch sits on the 15 m saddle where the road leaves the wet ground west of the crest, the lowest dry crossing of the old wall line.
why.whyNeighbours: The guard tower adjoins its northern pier and the broken curtain runs on from both piers, so the gate reads as part of a wall rather than a lone arch.
why.playerPurpose: The threshold of the city on foot, where the council patrol stands and asks for a licence.
why.microGeography: The road climbs 2 m through the arch; the ground under the piers is a firm 14–15 m shelf between the pond on the west and the crest on the east.

parcels.orientationWhy: The tower shares the arch's bearing, so its faces sit flush with the gate piers and the curtain beyond. Nothing turns on a doorway here, because the piece has none.

why.what: The squat Imperial gate tower, 6 m square and 13 m high, adjoining the north pier of the arch. It is a mass: the mesh has no room inside it.
why.whyHere: The Imperial wall had a tower at each gate; this one did not fall in 4E 48 and the council patrol uses it as its post.
why.whySpot: It stands on the north side of the arch, on the same shelf, where a watcher on its top sees the whole length of the road back to the pond.
why.whyNeighbours: The arch on its south and the broken curtain on its north are the pieces that it was built to join.
why.playerPurpose: The patrol post at the gate and the station for the north-gate quest scenes. The piece measures solid, so the tower is a thing to climb past rather than enter.
why.microGeography: Its footing falls 3 m across the base from the crest side to the road, so the tower is cut into the shelf, as the Imperial masonry here sank rather than stood on piles.

parcels.abutsWhy: The Morrowind Imperial keep set is authored so a guard tower butts the pier of its wall gate; the two pieces share a face.

parcels.orientationWhy: It continues the line of the tower northward, on the bearing of the old curtain.

why.what: A broken length of the Imperial curtain running north from the gate tower, its top fallen.
why.whyHere: The curtain ran from the gate up onto the crest; this is the piece that still stands next to the tower.
why.whySpot: It occupies the wall line immediately north of the tower, on the same shelf.
why.whyNeighbours: It joins the tower on one side and the standing west curtain on the other.
why.playerPurpose: A climbable stub that gives a view over the pond and back along the road.
why.microGeography: Its base steps up 0.5 m along the shelf toward the crest.

parcels.abutsWhy: A curtain segment is authored to butt the tower face in the Imperial keep set.

parcels.orientationWhy: It continues the line of the south pier of the arch, on the bearing of the old curtain.

why.what: A broken length of the Imperial curtain running south from the arch toward the pond.
why.whyHere: The curtain south of the gate ran down to the water; this is the piece that remains above ground.
why.whySpot: It sits on the wall line south of the arch, where the shelf begins to fall toward the pond.
why.whyNeighbours: It joins the arch on its north and ends at the rubble of the fallen south tower.
why.playerPurpose: It closes the gate yard on the south, so the road is the way into the city.
why.microGeography: The ground under it falls 0.6 m southward toward the pond.

parcels.abutsWhy: A curtain segment is authored to butt the gate pier in the Imperial keep set.

parcels.orientationWhy: The heap lies down the slope toward the pond, the direction in which the tower fell.

why.what: The rubble of the southern gate tower, an 11 m spread of ashlar left where it dropped.
why.whyHere: The gate had two towers; the southern one came down in the fighting of 4E 48 and the council has not cleared it.
why.whySpot: It lies at the south end of the wall line, on the falling ground between the curtain and the pond.
why.whyNeighbours: It marks the end of the wall stub and the edge of the pond.
why.playerPurpose: A find for a searcher: the tower stair is still open inside the heap.
why.microGeography: The heap has settled into ground that falls 3 m toward the pond, which is why the tower fell that way.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorway on one fixed side, so the parcel is turned until that doorway faces court path.

why.what: The tree-minder’s lodge, a bamboo hut on the west side of the court.
why.whyHere: The minder’s post rotates and whoever holds it must sleep within sight of the tree.
why.whySpot: It stands on the crest west of the court ring, 28 m from the trunk, outside the poles but facing the opening.
why.whyNeighbours: The second tender’s lodge sits on the opposite side of the court, so the two watchers are never in the same house.
why.playerPurpose: The minder’s home; the minder is the neutral broker of the city’s disputes.
why.microGeography: The crest here is 19–20 m and nearly level; the piles are short and the floor sits a step above the court.

parcels.orientationWhy: Yaw set by the shipped doorway, which opens onto tender path.

why.what: The second tender’s lodge, a bamboo hut on the north side of the court.
why.whyHere: City rule requires a second tender present whenever the minder listens to the tree.
why.whySpot: It stands on the northern edge of the crest, 36 m from the trunk, where the ground begins to fall toward the bench.
why.whyNeighbours: It is placed across the court from the minder’s lodge; the two doors face each other over the tree.
why.playerPurpose: The second witness in every Hist scene; the tender keeps the vigil roster.
why.microGeography: The crest falls 3 m across this hull toward the north, so the northern piles are longer than the southern.

parcels.orientationWhy: The open side of the awning faces the trunk, so the sitter watches the tree and not the court entrance.
parcels.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/argonian/orcawninghalf01

why.what: An open hide awning on four poles inside the court, where the vigil is sat.
why.whyHere: The vigil is kept in the open, in sight of the tree and of anyone entering the court.
why.whySpot: It stands inside the eastern opening of the court ring, 16 m south-east of the trunk.
why.whyNeighbours: The court footpath from the spine passes its north side to the tree.
why.playerPurpose: The seat for the Hist court scene and the place where the minder receives visitors.
why.microGeography: The awning stands on the level top of the crest at 21 m.

parcels.orientationWhy: The long axis follows the council walkway. At 259.8 deg the hall's open front looks down its own plank landing to the walk, so the sitting is entered from the front rather than off the bench grass.

why.what: The council hall, the tallest stilt house in the city, 18 m long and three storeys under its ridge. Its veranda front is the side in which the BM&V hall carries its door.
why.whyHere: The merchant council needs a covered floor for its sittings and a place for the tariff clerks.
why.whySpot: It stands on the 12 m bench north of the walkway, the widest level ground on the shoulder.
why.whyNeighbours: The record room is on its west, the strongroom behind it and the open council floor across the walkway.
why.playerPurpose: The council-hall station, the council-floor scene and the factor who gives the tariff quests.
why.microGeography: The bench falls 1 m to the north under the hull; the rear piles are longer.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so its own doorway gives onto bench walk, the way that runs past the plot.

why.what: The record room, a bamboo hut holding two centuries of customs books.
why.whyHere: The tariff is the council’s authority and its rolls have to be kept where the clerks sit.
why.whySpot: It is the first building on the bench west of the hall, where the spine arrives from the court.
why.whyNeighbours: The hall is its neighbour to the east; the strongroom is behind both.
why.playerPurpose: The tariff roll and the customs books that settle property claims.
why.microGeography: Level 12 m ground; the piles are short and even.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to put the shipped doorway on strongroom path.

why.what: The council strongroom, a bamboo hut behind the hall with the bonded goods inside.
why.whyHere: Goods held against unpaid duty need a locked room under the council’s eye.
why.whySpot: It stands behind the hall on the north edge of the bench, out of sight of the walkway.
why.whyNeighbours: The hall screens it from the market; the north curtain ruin lies beyond it.
why.playerPurpose: The strongroom loot and the pre-rebuild plan.
why.microGeography: The bench drops 1.5 m to the north here, so the rear piles stand in the fall.

parcels.orientationWhy: The deck lies along the walkway so stalls on it face the passing traffic.
parcels.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/kothringi/stilthouseplatform

why.what: The upper walkway market: an open deck on piles with no walls. Its outline is a plain rectangle because it is a platform.
why.whyHere: The record says the upper market stands on the walkways above the quay, out of the flood.
why.whySpot: It is set south of the walkway where the bench begins to fall, so the deck stands level over the slope.
why.whyNeighbours: The hall faces it across the walkway; the elders’ house is the next building east.
why.playerPurpose: The upper-market station, the traders and the rumour pool of the city.
why.microGeography: The ground under the deck falls 2 m southward; the south piles are the longest on the bench.

parcels.orientationWhy: The doorway is fixed on the hut, so the hut faces strongroom path.

why.what: The elders’ house, where the retired Shadowscales who settle disputes are found.
why.whyHere: In Lilmoth people look to their elders, including retired Shadowscales, for judgement.
why.whySpot: It stands on the walkway between the market deck and the council floor, in the middle of civic ground.
why.whyNeighbours: The market deck is west of it and the council floor east.
why.playerPurpose: The Retired Rota quest and a source of judgement outside the council.
why.microGeography: The crest bench is level here at 12 m, so the hut's stilts stand short and even.

parcels.orientationWhy: The stone ring is set to the fall of the bench edge into which it is dug, a few degrees off the walk, because a ring of stones follows its ground and not a survey.

why.what: The council floor, a ring of standing stones open to the sky.
why.whyHere: The council sits in the open when it rules on a tariff, so the ruling is seen.
why.whySpot: It stands at the east end of the bench beside the bell, where the quay is in view below.
why.whyNeighbours: The bell kiosk is next to it; the elders’ house is on its west.
why.playerPurpose: The council-floor scene and the council-standing mark.
why.microGeography: The stones are set into the fall at the south edge of the bench, which drops 2 m across the ring.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorway on one fixed side, so the parcel is turned until that doorway faces bench walk.

why.what: The council factor’s house, a bamboo hut east of the hall.
why.whyHere: The factor who holds the tariff line lives on the bench, within a few steps of the hall.
why.whySpot: It fills the gap between the hall and the bell, on the north side of the walkway.
why.whyNeighbours: The hall is on its west and the bell kiosk on its east.
why.playerPurpose: The quest-giver of the tariff line, at home in the evening.
why.microGeography: The bench falls about a metre northward under the plot. The stilts on the north side are the longer pair.

parcels.orientationWhy: The kiosk is set on the walkway's bearing so the bell hangs over the lip of the bench toward the quay. At 80.4 deg its access gap looks back down the walk that a climber has just come up.

why.what: The tariff bell: a 21 m timber kiosk tower on the lip of the bench, with the bell and a lamp at its top.
why.whyHere: The bell is rung when the tariff changes and when a hull lies at the roadstead; it has to be heard on the quay.
why.whySpot: It stands at the east end of the bench, 9 m above the flat, where the tower top is 30 m over the water.
why.whyNeighbours: The council floor and the factor’s house are beside it; the bluff stair leaves from its foot.
why.playerPurpose: The first thing seen from the bay and the mark that leads from the quay up to the council.
why.microGeography: The piles stand on the break of slope on 9–10 m ground; the lamp platform rides above it.

parcels.orientationWhy: Its long axis lies along the bluff foot, 8 deg off the west lane, so the building fits the strip between the slope and the lane. The veranda front looks east; a short landing carries the lane to it.

why.what: The tall block of Pusbottom, a three-storey stilt house against the bluff foot, let by the room.
why.whyHere: Pusbottom was repopulated by people who could pay for a room and not for a house.
why.whySpot: It stands at the north-west corner of the district, where the bluff shelters it and the stair from the bench comes down.
why.whyNeighbours: The west lane of the loop passes its east side; the stair foot is at its north end.
why.playerPurpose: The rooming house of the slum: hired rooms, the vault entrance quest and the broker’s office.
why.microGeography: The flat here is 2–3 m and the bluff rises behind it; the piles are level with the walkway.

parcels.orientationWhy: Yaw set by the shipped doorway, which opens onto pusbottom loop. It is canted a few degrees off its neighbours so the lane does not read as a drawn row.

why.what: A bamboo hut whose floor hides the shaft down to the flooded municipal vault.
why.whyHere: The old vault lies under this part of the flat. Whoever holds the hut holds the way down.
why.whySpot: It is the first hut on the west side of the loop, hard against the bluff foot where the vault roof is shallowest.
why.whyNeighbours: The tall block is to its north; the slaughter-list house is across the lane.
why.playerPurpose: The way into the Vault Beneath Pusbottom.
why.microGeography: The ground is 2 m and firm; the shaft goes down through the old fill.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so its own doorway gives onto pusbottom loop, the way that runs past the plot. A few degrees of cant off its neighbours keeps the lane from reading as a drawn row.

why.what: A bamboo hut in which a list of the names from the Slaughter is kept.
why.whyHere: Somebody in Pusbottom wrote down who died in 4E 48. The list stayed in the family.
why.whySpot: It stands on the east side of the west lane, opposite the vault house.
why.whyNeighbours: The vault house faces it; the agent’s room is two doors south.
why.playerPurpose: The slaughter-list evidence for the main quest.
why.microGeography: Level 2 m ground; the piles are a hand above the wet-season mark.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to put the shipped doorway on pusbottom loop.

why.what: The house of the broker who sells deeds to emptied Rockpark houses.
why.whyHere: Deeds to plague houses sell in a slum, where buyers ask few questions.
why.whySpot: It is the second hut on the west side of the loop, under the bluff.
why.whyNeighbours: The vault house is north of it and the reed-cutter’s house south.
why.playerPurpose: The Untouched House quest begins at this door. The broker will price a Rockpark deed for anyone who asks.
why.microGeography: The bluff foot keeps the ground here dry at 2 m.

parcels.orientationWhy: The doorway is fixed on the hut, so the plot is turned to 330° to bring it onto the west side of the Pusbottom loop.

why.what: A rented room in a bamboo hut, kept by the deniable An-Xileel agent.
why.whyHere: An agent of the successor state cannot live openly in a city that hates it; a room in Pusbottom is the cover.
why.whySpot: It is on the east side of the west lane, one door south of the slaughter-list house.
why.whyNeighbours: The broker’s house faces it across the lane.
why.playerPurpose: The agent quest-giver and the Pusbottom Remembers confrontation.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m, like its neighbours.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorway on one fixed side, so the parcel is turned until that doorway faces pusbottom loop. It stands a few degrees off the yaw of the plots either side of it.

why.what: A reed-cutter’s hut, with the cut reeds stacked under the floor.
why.whyHere: The reed fringe south of the quay is cut by Pusbottom households for thatch and matting.
why.whySpot: It is the third hut on the west side, where the bluff begins to draw back from the lane.
why.whyNeighbours: The broker’s house is north of it and the poler’s hut south.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter; the cutter knows the reed fringe and what lies in it.
why.microGeography: The flat is 2 m here and floods a hand deep at the wet-season peak.

parcels.orientationWhy: Yaw set by the shipped doorway, which opens onto pusbottom loop. The plot is set a few degrees off its neighbours, so the lane is not a straight row.

why.what: The house of the family who recognised their own goods in a licensed salvage lot.
why.whyHere: Salvage from the drowned quarter comes up under licence; the drowned owners’ heirs live in Pusbottom.
why.whySpot: It is the third hut on the east side of the west lane.
why.whyNeighbours: The agent’s room is north of it and the dice-runner’s hut south.
why.playerPurpose: The Licensed Lot quest begins here, with the family who recognised their own goods in the salvage sale.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m, a hand above the wet-season mark.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so its own doorway gives onto pusbottom loop, the way that runs past the plot. It is canted a few degrees off its neighbours so the lane does not read as a drawn row.

why.what: A poler’s hut, home to one of the lighter crews.
why.whyHere: The lighter crews live in Pusbottom because it is the cheapest ground within reach of the quay.
why.whySpot: It is the fourth hut on the west side of the loop.
why.whyNeighbours: The reed-cutter is north of it and the south-corner hut beyond.
why.playerPurpose: A crew member who carries the offer in the lighter-licensing quest.
why.microGeography: The flat is 1.5–2 m here and the piles are a little longer.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to put the shipped doorway on pusbottom loop. A few degrees of cant off its neighbours keeps the lane from reading as a drawn row.

why.what: The hut of the runner who carries stakes to the dice barge.
why.whyHere: The dice tables are on a barge outside the city; their business in the city runs through this door.
why.whySpot: It is the fourth hut on the east side of the west lane, nearest the south corner.
why.whyNeighbours: The lot-family house is north of it; the cross-lane huts are behind it.
why.playerPurpose: The Barge Debt and Cargo Off the Ledger quests.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m at the south corner of the loop, where the lane turns back towards the cross lane.

parcels.orientationWhy: The doorway is fixed on the hut, so the hut faces pusbottom loop. Its yaw is a few degrees off the plots either side, so the lane bends.

why.what: The last hut on the west lane, at the south-west corner of the loop.
why.whyHere: A household on the corner watches both the lane and the shore boardwalk.
why.whySpot: It is where the west lane turns east, on the edge of the district.
why.whyNeighbours: The poler’s hut is north of it; the shore lane to the fishers leaves at the corner.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling; the household saw who went out on the shore lane at night.
why.microGeography: The flat is 1–2 m and the hut stands on the highest of the low ground.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorway on one fixed side, so the parcel is turned until that doorway faces pusbottom cross.

why.what: A bamboo hut on the cross lane, home to a quay porter.
why.whyHere: The porters who carry from the lighters live nearest the quay.
why.whySpot: It is the first hut on the cross lane, just south of the spine.
why.whyNeighbours: The spine passes its north side; the next porter’s hut is south.
why.playerPurpose: A porter's dwelling to enter. It is the first door on the cross lane for a player coming off the spine.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m, a few steps from the quay deck.

parcels.orientationWhy: Yaw set by the shipped doorway, which opens onto pusbottom cross. It is canted a few degrees off its neighbours so the lane does not read as a drawn row.

why.what: A porter's hut on the cross lane, one of a shift of four who work the lighters together.
why.whyHere: The cross lane holds the porters’ households, who work the quay in shifts.
why.whySpot: It is the second hut on the cross lane, between the first porter's hut and the diver's.
why.whyNeighbours: Porters live on both sides of it and the east lane runs behind its back wall.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter. The quay shift sleeps here by day.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m, on the same flat that carries the whole cross lane.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so its own doorway gives onto pusbottom cross, the way that runs past the plot. The parcel is turned a few degrees against its neighbours; the lane is not a drawn row.

why.what: A hut on the cross lane kept by a diver who works the drowned quarter.
why.whyHere: The free-divers of the salvage yard live in Pusbottom and walk to the diving stair.
why.whySpot: It is the third hut on the cross lane, level with the divers’ shed on the quay.
why.whyNeighbours: Porters live north of it; the last cross-lane hut is south.
why.playerPurpose: A diver who knows the drowned hall and the Second Room quest.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m, level with the divers' shed across on the quay.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to put the shipped doorway on pusbottom cross. A small cant, a few degrees against the plots either side, keeps the lane off a straight line.

why.what: The last hut on the cross lane, home to a family of six.
why.whyHere: The cheapest ground in the city fills first with the largest families.
why.whySpot: It is the southern end of the cross lane, near the south corner of the loop.
why.whyNeighbours: The diver’s hut is north of it; the south-lane huts are round the corner.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter. Six live under this roof, the largest household in Pusbottom.
why.microGeography: The flat runs 1.5 to 2 m here and takes standing water at the south corner in the wet season.

parcels.orientationWhy: The doorway is fixed on the hut, so the plot is turned to 60° to bring it onto the south lane of the loop.

why.what: A bamboo hut on the south lane of the loop, facing the shore.
why.whyHere: The south lane is the edge of the district, where the newest arrivals build.
why.whySpot: It stands south of the lane between the west corner and the cross lane.
why.whyNeighbours: The south-corner hut is west of it and the second south hut east.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter, kept by one of the newest households in the district.
why.microGeography: Level 2 m ground open to the south, with no building between the hut and the shore.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorway on one fixed side, so the parcel is turned until that doorway faces pusbottom loop.

why.what: The second hut on the south lane, kept by a salvage sorter.
why.whyHere: The salvage yard’s sorters live nearest the yard, at the south-east of the district.
why.whySpot: It stands south of the lane near the south-east corner of the loop.
why.whyNeighbours: The first south hut is west of it; the salvage bench is round the corner to the north-east.
why.playerPurpose: A sorter who handled the weighted lot in A Body in the Lot.
why.microGeography: Level ground at 2 m on the south edge of the flat.

parcels.orientationWhy: The deck lies along the water line so the whole of its east side is quay.
parcels.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/kothringi/stilthouseplatform

why.what: The lighter quay: an open deck on piles at the water’s edge, 18 m along the shore. Its outline is a plain rectangle because it is a platform, not a house.
why.whyHere: Cargo comes ashore by lighter because the shelf is too shallow for a hull; this deck is where it is landed.
why.whySpot: It stands where the tidal flat gives out into the shelf, the nearest point to the channel that a deck reaches on piles.
why.whyNeighbours: The spine, the loop and the quay lane all end on it; the pier leaves its east side.
why.playerPurpose: The arrival point by boat, the lighter-quay station and the busiest ground in the city.
why.microGeography: Its west piles stand on the flat at 1 m and its east piles in the shallows.

parcels.orientationWhy: The kiosk is turned so its lamp face looks down the channel to the roadstead, which puts the access gap on the quay lane: the keeper climbs from the lane, the light shows to the water.

why.what: The quay lamp: a 21 m timber kiosk tower at the north end of the quay, lit at night.
why.whyHere: The lighters run at night when a hull lies at the roadstead and need a mark on which to steer.
why.whySpot: It stands on the water’s edge north of the deck, where its light is not hidden by the deck traffic.
why.whyNeighbours: The quay lane passes its west side; the lighter shed is across the lane.
why.playerPurpose: The lower of the two lamp tiers seen from the bay; the Whoever Relights It quest has its stair here.
why.microGeography: The piles stand on the flat at 0–1 m, a stride from the water.

parcels.orientationWhy: Yaw set by the shipped doorway, which opens onto quay lane.

why.what: The licence house, where lighter crews and divers are licensed and the dues are paid.
why.whyHere: The council licenses the lighters and the salvage; the licences are issued where the crews land.
why.whySpot: It is the northernmost building on the quay lane, the first door that a crew reaches from the deck.
why.whyNeighbours: The lighter shed is south of it and the lamp across the lane.
why.playerPurpose: Licensing the Lighters, the diving licences behind the salvage quests and the notice of dues.
why.microGeography: Firm 2 m ground at the foot of the slope from the bench.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so its own doorway gives onto quay lane, the way that runs past the plot.

why.what: The lighter shed, where landed cargo waits under a roof for the porters.
why.whyHere: Cargo landed at night cannot sit on the open deck in the rain.
why.whySpot: It is between the licence house and the deck, on the west side of the quay lane.
why.whyNeighbours: The deck is a few steps south; the licence house is north.
why.playerPurpose: The store in which cargo off the ledger is found.
why.microGeography: The quay flat runs 1 to 2 m here, level enough for a cargo barrow between the shed door and the deck.

parcels.orientationWhy: The shipped doorway of this composite looked out over open water, where no threshold can stand. The shed is turned so its door opens onto the made deck behind it.

why.what: The divers’ shed, where the salvage divers keep their lines and weights.
why.whyHere: The drowned quarter is worked by free-divers under licence; their yard is on the quay.
why.whySpot: It stands at the water’s edge south of the deck, where the diving stair drops into the channel.
why.whyNeighbours: The salvage bench is south of it; the east lane of the loop runs past its door.
why.playerPurpose: The diving-stair station and the dive-master who opens the drowned quarter.
why.microGeography: The flat is 0–1 m here; the piles on the water side stand in the shallows.

parcels.orientationWhy: The shipped doorway looked out over open water, where no threshold can stand. The bench is turned so its door opens onto the deck behind it, clear of the loop walk.

why.what: The salvage bench, where lots brought up from the drowned quarter are sorted and tagged.
why.whyHere: Salvage is the second living of the city after the lightering. It is sold sorted.
why.whySpot: It is the last building on the east lane, at the south end of the quay.
why.whyNeighbours: The divers’ shed is north of it; the south corner of the loop is beyond.
why.playerPurpose: The sorted lots of the Licensed Lot and A Body in the Lot quests.
why.microGeography: The flat is at 0–1 m; the reed fringe begins south of the hut.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 60° to put the shipped doorway on the shore lane, with the blank end wall to the boat awning.

why.what: A fisher’s hut at the west end of the row.
why.whyHere: The fishers of the estuary live on the low flat south of the bluff, near their boats.
why.whySpot: It is the westernmost hut of the row, beside the boat awning.
why.whyNeighbours: The boat awning is west of it and the second fisher’s hut east.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter; the fisher keeps the offering season.
why.microGeography: The flat is 2 m and drains slowly, so the westernmost plot of the row stands wet longest after a high tide.

parcels.orientationWhy: The doorway is fixed on the hut, so the hut faces shore lane. It is canted a few degrees off its neighbours so the lane does not read as a drawn row.

why.what: A fisher’s hut in the middle of the south row.
why.whyHere: The row holds the households who fish the shelf and the estuary mouth.
why.whySpot: It is the second hut of the south row, on the highest ground the row has.
why.whyNeighbours: Fishers live on both sides of it and the drying rack stands behind its south wall.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter. The row's boats are counted out from this door at dawn.
why.microGeography: The flat is 2–3 m here, the highest of the row.

parcels.orientationWhy: The composite carries its doorway on one fixed side, so the parcel is turned until that doorway faces shore lane. A few degrees of cant off its neighbours keeps the lane from reading as a drawn row.

why.what: A fisher’s hut, with the fish rack behind it.
why.whyHere: The catch is dried on the flat behind the houses, away from the walkway.
why.whySpot: It is the third hut of the south row, with the rack on its south side.
why.whyNeighbours: The rack stands behind it; fishers live either side.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter; the drying rack is the household’s trade.
why.microGeography: Level flat at 2 m, with the rack ground behind it.

parcels.orientationWhy: Yaw set by the shipped doorway, which opens onto shore lane. It is set a few degrees off the neighbouring plots.

why.what: The easternmost fisher’s hut, nearest the pole wall.
why.whyHere: The household nearest the estuary keeps the pole wall in repair.
why.whySpot: It is the last hut of the south row, 20 m from the water.
why.whyNeighbours: The pole wall is east of it and the third fisher’s hut west.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter; the keeper of the pole wall.
why.microGeography: The flat is 1.5–2 m and floods in the wet season.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so its own doorway gives onto shore lane, the way that runs past the plot.

why.what: A fisher’s hut on the north side of the shore lane.
why.whyHere: The row is two deep where the flat is widest.
why.whySpot: It stands north of the lane opposite the first two south huts.
why.whyNeighbours: The south row faces it across the shore lane. The bluff foot is behind it.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter, on the drier northern side of the lane.
why.microGeography: Level 2 m flat, drier than the south row.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 240° to put the shipped doorway on the shore lane, so the north row's doors face the south row's across it.

why.what: A fisher’s hut on the north side of the lane, kept by a recitation speaker.
why.whyHere: Two of the six speakers for the Sixth Recitation now work the quay and live in the shore quarter.
why.whySpot: It is the middle hut of the north side, opposite the second hut of the south row.
why.whyNeighbours: Fishers live on either side; the bluff rises 60 m to the north.
why.playerPurpose: The Sixth Recitation quest begins here, at the door of one of the six speakers.
why.microGeography: Level flat at 2 m under the bluff, which rises 60 m behind the plot.

parcels.orientationWhy: The doorway is fixed on the hut, so the hut faces shore lane. Its yaw is a few degrees off the plots either side, so the lane bends.

why.what: The easternmost hut of the north side, where the lane bends to the loop.
why.whyHere: The household on the bend sees everyone who comes down from Pusbottom.
why.whySpot: It stands where the shore lane turns north-east toward the loop corner.
why.whyNeighbours: The fourth south hut is opposite; the mangrove wall is beyond the pole wall.
why.playerPurpose: A dwelling to enter; the witness in the Half-Day Detour rumour.
why.microGeography: The flat is 2 m and the lane bends round a wet patch here.

parcels.orientationWhy: The open side faces the lane end, so a hull is carried in from the planks.
parcels.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/argonian/orcawninghalf01

why.what: A hide awning on poles under which the fishers’ canoes are repaired.
why.whyHere: Hulls have to be worked out of the rain. The fishers own no shed.
why.whySpot: It stands at the west end of the shore lane, where the lane stops.
why.whyNeighbours: The first fisher’s hut is east of it; the flat runs empty to the west.
why.playerPurpose: The end of the shore lane, where a canoe is borrowed for the estuary.
why.microGeography: Level flat at 2 m at the west end of the row.

parcels.orientationWhy: The ridge block keeps the 24° line of the old Imperial street, on which the villas of the lower town were set out.

why.what: A hollow Imperial block set so its top breaks the surface: the ridge that shows there is a city under the water.
why.whyHere: Old Imperial Lilmoth sank where it stood; this block stands nearest the quay in the shallowest water.
why.whySpot: It sits 30 m off the quay lamp in 1–2 m of water, north of the channel.
why.whyNeighbours: The channel passes south of it; the villa’s northern block lies further out.
why.playerPurpose: The long-range cue of the drowned quarter and the first thing a swimmer reaches.
why.microGeography: The bed is 1–2 m under the surface; the block’s upper courses stand clear at low water.

parcels.orientationWhy: The block keeps the old street grid of Imperial Lilmoth at 24°, which ran at a slant to the channel cut later through it.

why.what: A hollow block of a drowned villa, its roof gone, north of the channel.
why.whyHere: The villas along the old Imperial street sank into the shelf and have not been cleared.
why.whySpot: It lies on the old street line, 70 m off the quay, in 3–4 m of water.
why.whyNeighbours: The ridge block is inshore of it and a rubble floor beside it.
why.playerPurpose: A swim-through room with a salvage find inside it.
why.microGeography: The bed here is 3–4 m down and the block sits on the old street level.

parcels.orientationWhy: The rubble floor lies on the 24° street line, the last full course of a villa on the north side of the channel.

why.what: A walkable slab of villa floor on the bed, north of the channel.
why.whyHere: Where a villa collapsed, its floor remains as a standing surface.
why.whySpot: It lies east of the northern block on the old street grid.
why.whyNeighbours: The northern block is west of it and the roadstead beyond.
why.playerPurpose: A place to stand and surface between the northern block and the roadstead.
why.microGeography: The bed is 6–7 m down; the slab sits level on it.

parcels.orientationWhy: The southern rubble floor holds the same 24° street line, so the two floors read as one street across the channel cut.

why.what: A walkable stretch of villa floor south of the channel, 6 by 7 m.
why.whyHere: The southern villas fell flat when the shelf gave; their floors are the landing for divers.
why.whySpot: It lies 20 m south of the channel on the old street line.
why.whyNeighbours: The drowned hall is east of it and the diving stair inshore.
why.playerPurpose: The first landing on the dive from the stair to the hall.
why.microGeography: The bed is 9–10 m down here; the slab is the landing at the bottom of the dive.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hall is set to 24° with the rest of the drowned grid; its opening faces the diving stair on that bearing.

why.what: The hall of a drowned villa: a hollow block that a swimmer can enter and stand up inside.
why.whyHere: The largest villa on the old street had a hall; it is the room that the divers work first.
why.whySpot: It lies 95 m off the quay in 9–10 m of water, south of the channel.
why.whyNeighbours: The southern floor is inshore of it and the sunken shrine beyond.
why.playerPurpose: The drowned-quarter dive scene and the cleared mark.
why.microGeography: The bed is 9–10 m down; the block’s top is 5 m under the surface.

parcels.orientationWhy: The block lies along the slope of the bed, having slid off the street grid.

why.what: A villa block that slumped off the street line and lies askew on the bed.
why.whyHere: Not every villa sank square; this one slid toward the deeper water.
why.whySpot: It lies south-west of the hall, off the grid by 20 degrees.
why.whyNeighbours: The southern floor is north of it and the reed fringe inshore.
why.playerPurpose: A hiding place in the dive and a second salvage find.
why.microGeography: The bed is 9–10 m down here and the block lies along the old slope of the street.

parcels.orientationWhy: The opening faces west toward the diving stair, so a diver enters without turning.

why.what: The sunken shrine to Xhon-Mehl the Fisher: a hollow block with the idol, altar and marker inside.
why.whyHere: The fishers’ god of Lilmoth was worshipped in the lower town; the shrine drowned with it and the offerings continue.
why.whySpot: It is the outermost ruin, 120 m off the quay in 12 m of water, on the roadstead plateau.
why.whyNeighbours: The villa hall is inshore of it; the roadstead mark is north-east.
why.playerPurpose: The Offerings in the Mouth quest and the deepest dive from the city.
why.microGeography: The bed is 12 m down; the opening faces west toward the stair.

parcels.orientationWhy: The pane stands parallel to the quay lane and its face looks west across the lane at the licence house door, so a crew leaving the window reads it without turning.

why.what: A roofed timber notice board, 2.5 m high on two driven posts, with the posted dues and lot prices as part of the authored mesh.
why.whyHere: The licence house sets the dues; the crews read them here before they pay, which is the record's posted price list made a thing in the world.
why.whySpot: Across the lane from the licence house door and 11 m short of the quay lamp, where the lane is straight and the board can be read from either direction.
why.whyNeighbours: The licence house is the office behind it, the lamp lights it at night and the deck is thirty paces down the lane.
why.playerPurpose: The evidence surface for Cargo Off the Ledger: the posted dues against the tariff roll in the record room.
why.microGeography: On the dry flat at 2.3 m, clear of the lane's 2.5 m planks by a stride and a step above the flood band.

parcels.orientationWhy: The house is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the gate yard, which is the first open ground that a traveller reaches inside the wall.

why.what: The gate lodging, which rents beds and floor space by the night.
why.whyHere: A city that admits strangers at one gate has to house the ones who arrive after the boats have gone.
why.whySpot: It stands on the north side of the gate yard, inside the wall and before the spine begins.
why.whyNeighbours: The gate arch and the guard tower are its neighbours, so the watch sees who takes a bed.
why.playerPurpose: The bed that the player rents. It is also the room in which rumour about the quay is traded.
why.microGeography: Level fill behind the curtain wall, raised on a pad above the wet season line.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the spine track, which carries every load between the gate and the court.

why.what: The spine trader, which buys and sells everything that is not held under licence.
why.whyHere: Goods landed at the quay have to be sold somewhere that people walking in from the gate pass.
why.whySpot: It sits on the north verge of the spine track, at the point where the track straightens.
why.whyNeighbours: The tavern is a short walk east; the court palisade closes the view south.
why.playerPurpose: The general shop. It is also the fence for anything the licence house would have questioned.
why.microGeography: A stilt platform over soft ground beside the track, clear of the flood channel.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the court approach, which is the path that the tenders walk each morning.

why.what: The apothecary, which sells marsh remedies and buys what the cutters carry down.
why.whyHere: A city built over standing water keeps a trade in fever cures. That trade sits where the sap is watched.
why.whySpot: It stands on the north side of the court approach, outside the palisade that rings the Hist.
why.whyNeighbours: The tender lodges are the nearest houses, which is why the stock is trusted.
why.playerPurpose: Where poisons and cures are bought. It is also where the tenders can be asked about the tree.
why.microGeography: A stilt platform on the dry shoulder above the court ditch.

parcels.orientationWhy: The house is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the spine track, which is the way that the crews come up from the quay.

why.what: The tavern, which is the one roofed room in Lilmoth that is open to anybody who pays.
why.whyHere: Lighter crews paid off at the quay want a floor above the water before they walk home.
why.whySpot: It stands where the spine track bends south, halfway between the gate and the court.
why.whyNeighbours: The trader is west along the same track, so a crew spends its pay without leaving the spine.
why.playerPurpose: Drink, gossip and the hiring of hands. It is also the room in which the An-Xileel agent is found.
why.microGeography: A tall stilt frame on the deepest ground of the spine, which floods first and is therefore built highest.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hall is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the bench walk, which is the only approach that the council allows to the crown.

why.what: The guild hall, which the trading companies keep as their seat under the council.
why.whyHere: A council that licenses trade attracts the companies that pay for the licences. Those companies want a hall of their own.
why.whySpot: It stands at the west end of the bench walk, on the first rise of the council crown.
why.whyNeighbours: The council hall stands further along the same walk, close enough that a company's business is done in one morning.
why.playerPurpose: Where a faction is joined, contracts are taken and trainers are found.
why.microGeography: The seaward shoulder of the crown, which is high enough to stay dry in the wet season.

parcels.orientationWhy: The shed is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the quay lane, which is the way that carries the broken ironwork to it.

why.what: The quay smith, which forges and mends the fittings that the lighters wear out.
why.whyHere: Chain, hoop and pin fail on a working quay faster than a hull can bring replacements from Soulrest.
why.whySpot: It stands on the landward side of the quay lane, upwind of the deck so that the smoke clears the cargo.
why.whyNeighbours: The lighter shed stands north along the lane and the deck lies east, which is the source of its work.
why.playerPurpose: Repairs, blades and the salvaged iron the divers bring up.
why.microGeography: A stilt platform on firm bank above the tide line, set back from the open deck.

parcels.orientationWhy: The shed is turned so that its own doorway gives onto the quay lane, with its open side towards the water from which the hulls are drawn.

why.what: The boatwright, which builds and mends the flat lighters that carry the roadstead trade.
why.whyHere: Lilmoth loads deep hulls by lighter, so the city has to keep its own lighters afloat.
why.whySpot: It stands on the water side of the quay lane, north of the deck where a hull can be drawn up.
why.whyNeighbours: The deck and the channel are its neighbours, because a hull cannot be carried far.
why.playerPurpose: Where a boat is bought, repaired and fitted before the player takes to the water.
why.microGeography: The tidal edge of the quay, piled to the bed so that the working floor stays level at low water.

routes.why: The last stretch of the Imperial road from Blackrose, surveyed straight to the gate arch, which stands across it.
The Imperial road inside the arch, running straight to the lantern at the foot of the crest, where Imperial Lilmoth ended and the Argonian track begins.
The worn track from the gate yard over the southern shoulder of the crest, passing the Hist court on its left hand, down to the council bench.
The tenders’ path from the spine round the south of the court ring to the minder’s door.
The short path from the spine through the opening in the court ring to the trunk.
The path from the spine north-west to the second tender’s lodge on the crest edge.
The path from the council walkway round the east end of the hall to the strongroom door.
The timber stair down the bluff from the bell to the Pusbottom junction, 9 m of fall in 35 m.
A plank path off the gate yard to the lodging door, because the yard is kept clear for carts and the beds are reached from its edge.
A short path off the spine to the tavern door, because the track carries the quay traffic and drinkers step aside for it.

The fishers' path: the worn line from the gate yard down the southern slope to the shore quarter, 120 m of walking where the loop and the shore lane cost 500. The fishing households take their catch up to the gate market by it; a walker at the gate sees the fishers' roofs below; the path runs where a walker's eye already goes.

canals.why: The dredged navigation line from the pier head to the roadstead, the one water deep enough for a laden lighter across the shelf.

boardwalks.why: The council walkway, the one surveyed line in the Argonian city, laid straight along the bench from the spine track to the bell.
The spine across the north of Pusbottom from the stair foot to the quay deck, the busiest planks in the city.

The loop walkway of Pusbottom: a west lane that follows the bluff foot and bends with it, a short south lane over the wet ground and an east lane on piles over the shallows back up to the quay deck. Planks run straight from pile to pile between eleven bends, so no leg of it is a ruled line and none of it is a worn path.
The cross lane, a skewed plank link from the west lane to the east lane across the middle of the quarter, so a hut on the far side is reached without walking the whole loop.
The quay lane along the water’s edge from the lantern at the stair foot past the licence house and the lamp to the deck.
The boardwalk from the south-west corner of Pusbottom over the wet flat to the fishers’ row and the boat awning.
The lighter pier from the quay deck east to the head of the channel, where the lighters come alongside.
The short pier from the divers’ shed to the diving stair.
The plank landing off the council walkway to the hall's own front, so the sitting is entered from the walkway and not off the bench grass.
The short landing that carries the loop's west lane to the rooming house's door, because the tenants come home in the dark and the bluff foot is mud.

fences.why: The standing Imperial curtain from the gate tower north up the west face of the crest, 13 m high, what the water and the An-Xileel left.
The broken north curtain along the shoulder above the council bench, fallen to half its height.
The ring of driven poles round the Hist court, closed on the north, west and south and open to the spine on the east: walled and open, as the city rule requires.
fences.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/kothringi/tamu_woodpole01

fences.why: The Argonian wall facing the estuary: a line of driven poles along the shore of the fishers’ quarter, the city’s wall on the side that the Imperials never built.
fences.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/kothringi/tamu_woodpole01

why.what: The third Hist of Lilmoth, a 24 m tree grown from a root fragment of the second.
why.whyHere: Lilmoth has its own Hist despite having no native tribe; the third tree grew where the second was cut.
why.whySpot: It stands on the top of the crest at 22 m, the highest ground in the city.
why.whyNeighbours: The court ring surrounds it on three sides and the two tenders’ lodges face it.
why.playerPurpose: The first thing seen from the road and the site of the Hist court scene.
why.microGeography: The crest is level for 20 m round the trunk before falling away on every side.

landmarks.notes: Kept: never cleared, never enclosed by one faction. Crown top 46 m above sea level.

why.what: A hist flower growing at the foot of the trunk.
why.whyHere: The flowers come up from the root and the tenders leave them.
why.whySpot: It grows on the north-west side of the trunk.
why.whyNeighbours: It is inside the court ring, between the trunk and the minder’s lodge.
why.playerPurpose: An offering component for the Hist scenes.
why.microGeography: Level crest at 22 m, in the shade of the trunk for most of the day.

why.what: An Argonian lantern cage on a pole at the head of the gate road.
why.whyHere: The road end is lit so a traveller arriving at dusk sees the way turns into the city.
why.whySpot: It stands where the Imperial road ends and the Argonian track begins.
why.whyNeighbours: The arch is 30 m west; the track climbs east from it.
why.playerPurpose: The light that marks the gate yard from the road after dark.
why.microGeography: The 16 m shelf at the foot of the crest.

why.what: An Argonian lantern cage at the north end of the quay lane.
why.whyHere: The lane between the licence house and the lamp is lit for the night lighters.

why.whyNeighbours: The channel runs from it to the pier head; the shrine lies south-west.
why.playerPurpose: The point at which a passenger from a ship transfers to a lighter; the end of the channel.
why.microGeography: Driven into the 10 m plateau where the shelf ends.

combatSpaces.why: The council patrol holds the gate yard when the hostility flip to hunted closes the city; the yard between the arch and the lantern is the open ground for that fight.
Cargo Off the Ledger and A Body in the Lot both end on the deck. The guarded flip puts the patrol here first.
Pusbottom Remembers and the vault heist can turn to a fight in the lanes; the two-metre planks between huts are the tight class.
The Second Room and Short of Divers put a predator in the drowned hall; the fight is underwater between the floor slab and the block.

approaches.sequence: From the road on the flat west of the pond the crown of the Hist shows over the trees on the crest, 40 m above the traveller. The road bends round the pond and the gate tower and the standing curtain hide the tree; the arch and the tower are what is seen. The road runs straight through the arch into the gate yard, holding its own bearing; the track then climbs the shoulder and the tree comes back on the left hand behind its ring of poles; at the top of the shoulder the bell kiosk shows ahead and the bay opens beyond it.
approaches.wayfinding: Keep the pond on the left and hold the road's line through the arch to the lantern, then follow the track uphill with the pole ring on the left until the bell shows ahead.
approaches.notes: The road arrives from the west-north-west; the city calls it the north gate because the road is the road north to Blackrose. The last 200 m bend twice, round the pond and over the shoulder.

approaches.fromDirection: east, from the roadstead in Oliis Bay
approaches.sequence: From a lighter at the roadstead the bell kiosk on the lip of the bench reads first, 30 m above the water, with the quay lamp below it and the Hist crown behind and higher. Along the channel the ridge block breaks the water on the right hand and hides the lamp for a moment; then the pier head, the quay deck and the sheds along the lane come into view under the bluff.
approaches.wayfinding: Steer for the upper lamp, keep the ridge block to starboard and come alongside at the pier head; the deck is the end of the pier and the stair up to the bell leaves from the lane behind it.
approaches.notes: The lighter takes the dredged line; a swimmer from the roadstead crosses the drowned quarter and reaches the diving stair first.

approaches.fromDirection: south, along the estuary shore from the high junction and the hist-less fringe
approaches.sequence: From the flat to the south the bell kiosk stands over the bluff and the Hist crown behind it. The pole wall and the fishers’ roofs hide the bluff foot as the walker comes up the shore; the shore lane appears between the pole wall and the mangrove; at the corner of Pusbottom the tall block and the lanes are seen close under the bell.
approaches.wayfinding: Walk the shore with the water on the right until the pole wall; the lane between the last fisher’s hut and the wall leads to the corner of the loop; the stair to the bell is at the far end of the west lane.
approaches.notes: The high junction tower at 3773, 6496 stands 15 m outside the pole wall and is the mid-way mark on this approach.

assetConstraints: settlement-mud-v1 is forbidden here: Lilmoth is Murkmire reed/stilt culture and material-culture.md forbids blending the two Argonian building cultures in one settlement.

composite:quay/stone-quay-with-stilt-house is forbidden here: it welds an Imperial keep stone dock to an Argonian stilt house, which is both the owner’s 2026-09-04 worked example of a composition nobody authored and a two-culture blend inside one mesh.

Dock systems are never butted mid-run: the BM&V Dagon Fel jetty system builds the lighter pier, HTBM’s tamu_ lashed-plank boardwalk builds the shore boardwalks; the change of system happens at the quay deck.
No new work is built into the Imperial masonry in district.lilmoth.north-gate.

networkTerminals.why: The Blackrose road runs in along the pond's north shore and reaches the bluff foot here, on the one line of firm ground between the pond and the tidal flat; the city walls its gate across that line, so the road and the gate yard inside are one street.

The Soulrest lane comes up the estuary from the west and can go no further than the channel head. The shelf inside is too shallow for a laden hull, so the run ends at the lighter quay and the pier carries the cargo up to the deck.

The Archon lane leaves from the berth at which it arrives. A boat bound north is loaded at the quay off the pier, so the lane starts where the pier ends rather than at a second landing that the city never built.

The Blackrose lane comes down out of the marsh from the north-west and joins the same channel head. Poled craft come alongside the quay from the landward side of the berth, so one quay serves all three lanes.
